newsitem.title: ITALY: Core investors sought for Telecom Italia.
newsitem.headline: Core investors sought for Telecom Italia.

text.p: The hunt is on for core investors to lead Telecom Italia after its privatisation later this year, but there are doubts over how many foreign firms will be let into the inner circle.
"The danger of colonialisation in our country is enormous," said Nerio Nesi, economic spokesman for the Communist Refoundation party which wants to keep firm control of the utility in Italian hands.
The state's 44 percent stake is due to be placed on the market in October in what is likely to be one of the world's biggest privatisations this year.
As in past Italian sales, most of the shares will be sold to retail and institutional investors, with the rest reserved for an elite of stable shareholders.

Among firms believed to be considering joining the stable core are the Agnelli family holding Ifil, banking group Istituto San Paolo di Torino, Germany's Mannesmann and U.S. telecommunications group AT&T.

No single company or investor will be able to hold more than three percent, with Italian newspapers speculating that around 15 percent of Telecom stock will be placed in the hands of the core investors.
An information pack has already been sent to a limited list of potential investors, the Treasury said on Friday, with interested parties expected to reply by September 2.
AT&T announced earlier this year it was forming a strategic alliance with Telecom Italia in a move many saw as a preliminary step towards joining the inner circle of investors.

But not everyone is happy with the idea of allowing foreign groups so close to the helm of such a strategic business. Telecom is the world's sixth largest phone operator by number of subscribers, and controls Europe's biggest mobile phone firm.
"We are against foreigners being let into the hard core of Telecom, unless there is a reciprocal agreement," said Nesi, referring to possible share swap arrangements.

Asked about the chances of such a swap with AT&T, a senior Telecom executive said last month that the Italian group was interested in taking stakes in "a galaxy of companies", but AT&T was not one of them.

The hard-left Refoundation secures Prime Minister Romano Prodi's parliamentary majority, and Nesi said at the weekend his group would not hesitate to try to block the Telecom sale if it thought the national interest was threatened.
While the inner core of shareholders can expect a large say in Telecom Italia's future direction, the government has already booked itself a "golden share" in the company.
This will give the Treasury power of veto for at least three years on key decisions such as acquisitions, asset disposals and choice of a core of stable shareholders.
With this protection in hand, the government sees no threat in allowing foreigners into the inner ring of shareholders.

"I believe (these firms) can meet the necessary standards," Industry Ministry Pierluigi Bersani was widely quoted as saying by the Italian media last week when asked if AT&T and Mannesmann would make suitable partners for Telecom.

However, with Refoundation flexing its muscles and centrist government party Italian Renewal also openly worried about AT&T buying into Telecom, some newspapers have suggested that its entry into the Italian telecom stable core might be delayed.
"It's an obstacle which might be put off to another time," La Repubblica daily said at the weekend.
